subject: efficient version of Gaussian Process fitting/prediction

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: efficient version of Gaussian Process fitting/prediction
parts:
Hi,

I messed up with the example on GP prediction in the manual (sec 12.4) and found a more efficient way to generate prediction using generated quantities.  I wonder if it is possible to improve the code even more - or I messed up. I am planning to use the code for a larger data set and different kernels so it would be good to have efficient code (or know that I am wrong).

Linas
SETest.stan is a more efficient code, SETest1.stan is the code from the manual, SETest.r is the R code to run both

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: efficient version of Gaussian Process fitting/prediction
parts: You don't have to construct the whole covariance matrix Sigma again in the generated quantities block. You could reuse Sigma1, if it would be declared in the transformed parameters block. For example, see Stan manual p. 98 "Analytical Form of Joint Predictive Inference".

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: efficient version of Gaussian Process fitting/prediction
parts:
I don't think that Cholesky decomposition helps, if you are taking just 1 sample in generated quantities. (it might be a good idea to sample more though)

For linearity, have you tried linear covariance function (more info: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process)? In that case, GP is basically equal to (Bayesian) linear regression. And then you could add flexibility to the model having covariances such as:  K_linear + K_squaredExp and so on.

Herra,

By multiple samples you mean y2, y3, ... I am little confused why.  I expect that quantiles of y2, y3, ... will be pretty much the same. Or this is not the case?

With respect to the second question.  The model I am trying to calibrate with experimental data is not linear (I used linear as an example).  I would like to model the case when I "believe" 100% in experimental data.  Then GP gives me a good prediction.  What to do if I "believe" 100% in model?  Or something in between?  For regression frequentists have weights.  I wonder if similar mechanism exists for calibration in Bayesian domain?
Thank you,
Linas
